newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: WTO chief calls on EU to lead trade liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: WTO chief calls on EU to lead trade liberalisation.

text.p: The head of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) called on Wednesday for the European Union to lead global economic integration, but cautioned the EU not to alienate developing countries by pursuing controversial issues.

Speaking at a dinner ahead of Thursday's EU trade ministers' meeting, WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero said the 15-nation bloc's open-market experience gave the world a blueprint for global free trade.
But he stressed that the EU could alienate less developed countries if it pushed its political principles too far.
The trade ministers are meeting to review positions to be taken by the European Union at the WTO ministerial meeting in Singapore in December.
Ruggiero is anxious that the agenda for Singapore remains focused on work in progress rather than becoming bogged down with so-called "new issues" such as labour standards.

"The European trade experience gives you a unique chance and a unique responsibility to take the lead in ensuring that the principles that have worked so well within Europe are also allowed to work well outside it," Ruggiero told the ministers.
"(Trade) was the key to bringing the peoples of Europe closer ... it is more and more doing the same job in the wider world."
Ruggiero said while he saw progress between the West and developing nations over labour standards, raising the issue at the WTO risked widening their differences.
Developing nations -- particularly those in Asia -- fear attempts by the EU and United States to impose western-style labour standards on their industries will reduce their competitive edge.

"We are dealing more with political positions and questions of atmosphere and perception," Ruggiero said. "In such a position, where the way to eventual consensus may be less clear, it becomes all the more important not to push particular positions too far."
Ruggiero called on developed countries to "act courageously" to bring about a further liberalisation of the world's textile and garment industries.

"There is considerable anxiety among textile exporting developing countries ... that the major importers are not always living up to the spirit of the Uruguay Round agreement, whatever their observance of the letter," he said.
"I think there is a case to answer here, and it is in the interests of Europe -- including its textile producers -- to be more forthcoming."
